To look at a star in passing glances—to see it from the corner of your eye, directing toward it the outer parts of the retina, which are more sensitive to faint light than the inner parts—is to see the star clearly and appreciate its brightness best. That brightness fades the more directly we look at it. In the latter case, more rays actually enter the eye; in the former, however, the ability to perceive them is more delicate. By thinking too deeply we confuse and weaken thought; even Venus can be made to disappear from the sky through observation that is too prolonged, too concentrated, or too direct.

“As for these murders, let us make some investigations ourselves before we form an opinion about them. An inquiry will give us some amusement”—I thought this a strange word to use, but said nothing—“and besides, Le Bon once did me a service for which I remain grateful. We will go and see the place for ourselves. I know G——, the chief of police, and should have no trouble getting the necessary permission.”

Permission was granted, and we left immediately for the Rue Morgue. It is one of those wretched streets lying between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We arrived late in the afternoon, since the district is a considerable distance from the one where we lived. We found the house easily: across the street, a number of people were still staring up at its closed shutters with aimless curiosity. It was an ordinary Parisian house with a gateway. Beside the gateway stood a glass-fronted booth with a sliding panel in its window, identifying it as the concierge’s lodge. Before entering, we walked farther up the street, turned down an alley, and turned again to pass behind the building. All the while, Dupin examined the entire neighborhood as well as the house with a painstaking attention whose purpose I could not begin to see.

We retraced our steps to the front of the house, rang the bell, and showed our credentials to the officers in charge, who admitted us. We went upstairs to the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body had been found and where both dead women still lay. As was customary, the room’s disorder had been left undisturbed. I saw nothing beyond what the Gazette des Tribunaux had described. Dupin examined everything closely, including the victims’ bodies. We then visited the other rooms and the yard, accompanied throughout by a police officer.

Well, I said I needed the watermelon. But he said I didn’t need it to escape from prison; that was the difference. He said if I’d wanted to hide a knife inside it and smuggle it to Jim so he could kill the steward, that would have been all right. So I left it there, though I couldn’t see the benefit of playing a prisoner if I had to sit and chew over a lot of fancy distinctions every time I got a chance to swipe a watermelon.

Well, as I was saying, that morning we waited until everyone had settled down to work and nobody was around the yard. Then Tom carried the sack into the lean-to while I stood some distance away, keeping watch. After a while he came out, and we went and sat on the woodpile to talk. He said:

“Everything’s sorted now except the tools, and that’s easy enough to fix.”

“Tools?” I said.

“Yes.”

“What for?”

“To dig with, of course. We’re not going to chew him out, are we?”

“Aren’t those old broken picks and things in there good enough to dig a Black man out with?” I said.

He turned toward me with enough pity in his face to make you cry, and said:

“Huck Finn, have you ever heard of a prisoner keeping picks and shovels and every modern convenience in his wardrobe to dig himself out with? Now let me ask you—if you’ve got any sense at all—what chance would that give him to be a hero? They might as well hand him the key and be done with it. Picks and shovels! They wouldn’t provide those even for a king.”

“Well, then,” I said, “if we don’t want picks and shovels, what do we want?”

“A couple of table knives.”

“To dig out the foundations under that cabin?”

“Yes.”

“Damn it, Tom, that’s foolish.”

“It doesn’t matter how foolish it is. It’s the right way, and it’s the usual way. There isn’t any other way I’ve ever heard of, and I’ve read all the books that tell you about these things. They always dig out with a table knife—and remember, it’s usually solid rock, not dirt. It takes them weeks and weeks and weeks, forever and ever. Take that prisoner in the lowest dungeon of the Castle Deef, in Marseilles harbor, who dug himself out like that. How long do you suppose he spent at it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Well, guess.”

“I don’t know. A month and a half.”

I remembered the way things had been during our great civil war of the nineteenth century. A carpenter in the North earned three dollars a day, reckoned in gold; in the South he earned fifty, paid in Confederate shinplasters that were worth a dollar a bushel. A suit of overalls in the North cost three dollars, or one day’s pay; in the South the price was seventy-five, or two days’ pay. Everything else followed the same proportion. Thus Northern wages were twice Southern wages, since one would purchase twice what the other would.

Yes, I struck up several acquaintances in the hamlet, and one discovery pleased me considerably: our new coins were circulating there. There were plenty of milrays, plenty of mills, plenty of cents, a fair number of nickels, and some silver, all passing among the craftsmen and the common people at large. Yes, there was even a little gold, though that was at the bank, which is to say the goldsmith’s. While Marco, the son of Marco, bargained with a shopkeeper for a quarter-pound of salt, I stepped into the bank and requested change for a twenty-dollar gold piece. They supplied it—after biting the coin, ringing it against the counter, testing it with acid, and asking where I had obtained it, who I was, where I came from, where I was headed, when I meant to arrive, and possibly two hundred other questions. When their questions ran dry, I kept going and volunteered a quantity of information: I possessed a dog named Watch; my first wife belonged to the Free Will Baptists; her grandfather was a Prohibitionist; I had once known a fellow with two thumbs on either hand and a wart inside his upper lip, who had died expecting a glorious resurrection; and so forth, and so forth, and so forth. At last even that ravenous village interrogator began to seem satisfied, and a little annoyed as well. Still, he was obliged to respect someone of my financial standing, so he offered me no impudence. I did observe that he vented his feelings on his subordinates, a perfectly natural proceeding. Yes, they changed the twenty, although I thought it put the bank under a slight strain. That was only to be expected: it was like entering a puny nineteenth-century village shop and suddenly asking its proprietor to break a two-thousand-dollar bill. Perhaps he could manage it; nevertheless he would wonder how a small farmer came to have so much money in his pocket. The goldsmith was probably wondering the same thing, for he accompanied me to the door and remained there, watching me depart with reverent admiration.
